newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil posts record trade gap in 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil posts record trade gap in 1996.

text.p: Brazil posted a record trade gap of $5.539 billion in 1996, with imports surging 6.88 percent and exports rising a sluggish 2.67 percent over the previous year, government officials said on Tuesday.
December's deficit was an unprecedented $1.787 billion, with imports at a highest-ever monthly level of $5.576 billion.

But Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros, economic policy secretary at the Finance Ministry, said Brazil could easily finance its 1996 current account gap and any shortfalls in its balance of payments over the next years.
"All is tranquil," Mendonca de Barros told reporters, citing Brazil's $60 billion in foreign reserves and a record inflow of foreign direct investment in 1996, estimated at $8.0 billion.
Mendonca de Barros also noted the quality of Brazilian overseas issues was improving, with Brazilian firms and sovereign debt gaining greater maturities and narrower spreads over U.S. Treasuries.
"We have our reserves and...foreign direct investment rose significantly. In 1997, I see more of the same," he said.
Brazil's 1996 current account deficit is expected to hit some 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.

Economic analysts reacted calmly to the size of 1996 trade deficit, which compared with forecasts of equilibrium at the beginning of the year, 1995's gap of $3.352 billion and a massive $10 billion surplus in 1994.

"It was a high number, considering that most of the deficit was concentrated in the second half of the year. At this pace, we will have a higher trade deficit in 1997 but we don't think it will be explosive or out of control," said Odair Abate, chief economist at Lloyds Bank, Brazil.
Analysts generally agreed with Mendonca de Barros's view that the current account deficit was manageable.
Economists surveyed by Reuters expect a $7.0-8.0 billion trade gap and an erosion in the current account deficit to about 3.3 percent of GDP in 1997.
The Finance Ministry's economic policy secretary said it was too early to tell how imports would perform in early 1997.

But he said there were clear signs importers had increased orders in December in anticipation of possible problems with the new SISCOMEX on-line import registration system, which became operative on January 1.
Mendonca de Barros said that factor added to others to boost imports at the end of last year and widen the trade gap.

The other elements were a surge in consumer demand in the second half of 1996 following looser credit policies as well as a boom in capital goods imports because of foreign investment in Brazilian companies and modernization by local firms.
"Even without tighter monetary policies, all the data points to a natural slowdown (in demand)," Mendonca de Barros said.

As for capital goods imports, which rose 12.1 percent in 1996 to $12.704 billion from $11.330 billion in 1995, he said they were "positive". "Foreign investment is welcome. It also points to a recuperation of competitiveness," he said.

Mauricio Cortes, foreign trade secretary at the Ministry of Industry and Commerce, said capital goods imports were heading for the textiles, shoes, timber, tobacco, furniture and electronics sectors. "All these sectors have a significant participation in Brazilian exports," Cortes said.
Mendonca de Barros and Cortes also blamed the wider-than-expected trade gap last year on fuel imports, which rose 33.6 percent, mainly in the last quarter of 1996.
They said the purchases were most likely due to increased consumer demand and would slow down along with the economy.
((-- Brasilia newsroom 55-61-2230358))
